acceptable.choice: Keep Node.js + TypeScript: run a separate WebSocket gateway deployment (ws or uWebSockets.js) spread over several pods
acceptable.why: 50,000 mostly idle sockets that carry presence and invite traffic is a modest load for Node across a handful of pods, and it keeps the system in the only stack the two people who will run it know well.

acceptable.choice: Socket.IO with its Redis adapter instead of raw ws
acceptable.why: It gives them rooms, acks, reconnection and cross-pod broadcast out of the box, which saves time before launch; the cost is more memory per connection and a Socket.IO client library in Unity.

acceptable.choice: Managed Redis/Valkey for presence (keys with a TTL, refreshed by heartbeats), cross-pod routing of invites (pub/sub), and the matchmaking queue (sorted sets with atomic Lua or transactions)
acceptable.why: Any pod can then deliver an invite to whichever pod holds the target's socket, and the realtime churn stays out of Postgres, using a managed piece the team can operate.

acceptable.choice: A single matchmaker worker in Node, separate from the gateways (one leader, or partitioned by region or game mode), that runs a tick every 250–500 ms over the Redis queue
acceptable.why: Matching the fraction of 50k players who are queued at any moment is a small amount of CPU, a periodic tick fits easily within 2 seconds, and a single owner per partition avoids matching the same player twice.

acceptable.choice: A managed matchmaking service (Unity Gaming Services Matchmaker, PlayFab, GameLift FlexMatch) behind the Node gateway
acceptable.why: It takes matchmaking off the two back-end developers and fits a Unity studio, as long as cost, lock-in and integration with their existing accounts are acceptable.

acceptable.choice: Nakama (open source game server with a TypeScript runtime and Postgres storage), self-hosted or as Heroic Cloud
acceptable.why: It ships presence, parties and matchmaking, and its server logic can be written in TypeScript, but it is a new system to operate and would mean moving accounts, so it fits only if launch is far enough away.

acceptable.choice: A managed WebSocket or pub/sub service (Ably, Pusher, AWS API Gateway WebSockets) holding the connections
acceptable.why: It takes connection holding and reconnect storms off the team's hands, at a per-connection or per-message price they need to estimate for 50k players online at once.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting realtime in Elixir/Phoenix before launch
ruled_out.why: Nobody on the team knows the language or the BEAM runtime, two people would have to operate it in production at launch, and Node already meets the load, so they would take on rewrite risk for headroom they don't need.

It is technically capable but means a new language and toolchain for the two operators, with no requirement here that Node can't meet; Go becomes worth considering only if load tests show a real limit.

ruled_out.choice: Building the realtime service in C# (ASP.NET Core SignalR) because the studio knows C#
ruled_out.why: The C# developers have never run servers, so the two Node developers would end up on call for a second back-end stack.

ruled_out.choice: A realtime server in C++ written by the engine programmer
ruled_out.why: It depends on one person, adds operational burden, and buys performance the situation doesn't need.

ruled_out.choice: One big Node process holding all 50k connections
ruled_out.why: It is a single point of failure at launch, and one crash or deploy disconnects every player at once.

ruled_out.choice: Presence and matchmaking state in each pod's memory with no shared bus
ruled_out.why: Once there is more than one pod, invites can't reach players connected to another pod and the matchmaker can't see the whole queue.

ruled_out.choice: Writing presence heartbeats to Postgres, or polling Postgres for invites and match queues
ruled_out.why: This puts constant write churn on the database that also serves accounts and inventory, which is how a launch falls over.

ruled_out.choice: HTTP polling instead of WebSockets for presence and invites
ruled_out.why: It conflicts with the stated WebSocket requirement and with player-facing latency, and it multiplies request load.

ruled_out.choice: Running the WebSocket gateway inside the existing REST API process
ruled_out.why: Every REST deploy or crash would then drop all player sockets, and long-lived connections would compete with request handling.

must_mention: Direct answer: yes, Node can handle 50k concurrent WebSockets plus 2-second matchmaking when it is scaled horizontally; a language rewrite isn't justified, and the risk lies in architecture and operations, not language speed.
Rough sizing: plan for 5–10k connections per pod over at least 3–4 pods plus headroom, with tens of KB of memory per connection, so a few GB in total; the real numbers have to be measured.
Players connected to different pods need a shared store or bus (typically managed Redis) for presence and invite routing.
Run matchmaking as a separate single-owner worker (or one per partition) with atomic queue operations so no player is matched twice, and keep heavy synchronous work off the gateway event loop.
Load-test before launch at 1.5–2x the expected peak (k6, Artillery or similar), including a mass-reconnect scenario and a matchmaking-queue spike, and measure p99 time to match.

Plan for reconnect storms: the Unity client needs reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and the server should verify a token (e.g., a JWT) on connect instead of hitting Postgres for every connection.

Kubernetes details for long-lived connections: load balancer and ingress idle timeouts, server ping/pong heartbeats, graceful drain on SIGTERM with a long enough terminationGracePeriod, PodDisruptionBudgets, and higher file-descriptor limits.
Autoscale gateways on connection count or memory, not CPU, and scale out before launch instead of relying on reactive autoscaling during the spike.
Protect Postgres from the login rush with connection pooling (PgBouncer or pool limits) and rate limiting, since the REST API is also part of what can fall over.
Observability for two operators: metrics for connections per pod, queue depth, time to match, and Redis/Postgres health, plus alerts and a runbook.
Elixir or Go would only make sense later, if measurements show a Node limit, and not as a launch decision.
red_flags: Recommending an Elixir or Go rewrite for launch based on benchmarks or reputation while ignoring that only two people will run it and neither knows the language.
Claiming Node can't handle 50k WebSockets because it is single-threaded.
Claiming Node handles it trivially, with no mention of load testing, horizontal scaling, or cross-pod routing.
Putting presence or matchmaking hot paths in Postgres.
Running the matchmaking loop on every gateway pod with no coordination, which causes duplicate or conflicting matches.
Ignoring deploys and pod restarts that drop sockets, and the reconnect storm that follows.
Proposing heavy infrastructure (Kafka, a service mesh, a custom distributed actor system, multi-region active-active) that two people can't operate before launch.
Assuming the C# developers can share on-call or operations for a new server stack.
Autoscaling WebSocket pods on CPU alone.
Recommending a managed service without noting its cost at 50k concurrent connections or the work of integrating it with the existing accounts system.
unknowns: How long until launch, which decides whether adopting Nakama or a managed service is realistic.
Presence fan-out: friend-list or party sizes and how often status changes, since each change is multiplied by the number of subscribers.
Matchmaking rules (skill brackets, party sizes, regions, latency-based matching) and how many players are in the queue at once and how fast they arrive.
Whether 2 seconds is a p99 or an average target, and what happens when no good match exists.
Whether players are in one region or several, which affects latency and whether the matchmaker needs partitioning.
Measured memory and CPU per connection with their chosen library and message sizes.
The managed load balancer's connection limits, idle timeouts, and WebSocket support on their cloud.
Expected login/connect rate at launch and in a mass reconnect, and how much Postgres can absorb.
Budget for managed Redis, matchmaking, or WebSocket services versus engineering time.
Whether a match must also allocate a dedicated game server (e.g., Agones or a vendor service), which adds to the 2-second budget and to operations.
